title: Pipelining in a processor
learner_summary: A student who has just started computer architecture. They know what an instruction is and that a processor runs one after another, but they have not yet learned how pipelining overlaps instructions, or why a pipeline can stall.

objectives.text: Explain why pipelining makes a processor faster: it overlaps instructions.
Explain why a pipeline stalls: a hazard, which is structural, data or control.
Explain how a pipeline handles a hazard: stalling or bypassing.

facts.text: Pipelining overlaps instructions: with 4 stages, 100 instructions take 4 + 99 = 103 cycles, against 400 cycles without overlap.
A hazard stops the pipeline when an instruction needs something that is not ready yet.
In ADDI R1, R0, #10 followed by ADDI R4, R1, #17, the second instruction needs R1 before the first has computed it, so there is a data hazard.
A structural hazard happens when two instructions need the same piece of hardware in the same cycle, so one of them has to wait.
A control hazard happens when an instruction has to wait for the result of a branch before the pipeline knows which instruction comes next.
A pipeline can stall, which means waiting until the result is ready.
A pipeline can bypass, which means sending the result directly to the instruction that needs it.

misconceptions.text: Every pipeline stall is a data hazard.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what the instruction is waiting for: the same piece of hardware is a structural hazard, the result of an earlier instruction is a data hazard, and the result of a branch is a control hazard.

misconceptions.text: Pipelining makes every single instruction faster.
misconceptions.correction: One instruction still takes the same time; what gets faster is the total throughput: 100 instructions go from 400 cycles to 103 cycles.
